title: Short Stuff: Alligator Gar
summary: Short Stuff episode on the alligator gar, a large prehistoric-looking freshwater fish native to North and Central America. Josh describes spotting a two-and-a-half-foot gar at a Georgia lake, then covers its ancient lineage (fossils up to about 100 million years old), the flattened, shovel-like snout that gives it its name, its two rows of upper teeth, and its size (typically around 6 feet and 160 pounds, with record fish reported up to about 10 feet and 350 pounds). He mentions a conservationist's video of an 8-foot catch and notes the fish is not considered good to eat, has armor-like ganoid scales, and has toxic roe. The hosts discuss its opportunistic diet, including playing dead to ambush prey, its harmlessness to people, its habitat preference for low-oxygen waters where it uses an air bladder to absorb oxygen, its slow maturation and spawning that make it vulnerable to overfishing and regulated in places like Florida, historical use of its scales for jewelry and tools, and the outdated belief that gar harm other fish populations. Josh closes with a reference to the Errol Morris documentary Vernon, Florida.

segments.title: Opening banter and spotting a garfish at a Georgia lake
segments.summary: Josh explains the episode's inspiration: he saw a large garfish near the surface of a lake in Georgia while about to jump in to cool off, and says garfish look prehistoric.

segments.title: Ancient lineage, name origin, and size
segments.summary: The hosts describe fossils up to about 100 million years old, the flattened snout that gives the alligator gar its name and Latin name Atractosteus spatula, the two rows of upper teeth, and typical and record sizes including a Texas record and a conservationist's 8-foot catch.

segments.title: Not good to eat
segments.summary: The hosts say alligator gar are not a good food fish because of their taste and armor-like ganoid scales, and that the roe is toxic in all gar species.

segments.title: Diet, ambush hunting, and safety around people
segments.summary: Alligator gar are opportunistic eaters that will take many prey animals, sometimes ambushing them by playing dead. The hosts note there are no recorded attacks on people.

segments.title: Habitat, oxygen use, and range
segments.summary: Gar are freshwater fish found only in North and Central America and prefer low-oxygen areas such as coves, backwaters, swamps, and bayous. Their air bladder helps them float and absorbs oxygen into the blood.

segments.title: Conservation, regulations, and historical uses
segments.summary: Gar mature slowly and spawn in specialized areas, making them vulnerable to overfishing; in Florida and elsewhere they are highly regulated. Early humans used their scales for jewelry and tools. The old belief that gar harmed other fish populations is described as wrong.

segments.title: Name origin and Vernon, Florida reference
segments.summary: Josh notes the name gar comes from an Anglo-Saxon word for spear and recalls a garfish character in the Errol Morris documentary Vernon, Florida.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts wrap up the short episode and sign off.
